prompt: What is needed for two machines to exchange data?
optionA: A browser on each machine
optionB: A connection between them and an agreed way of addressing each other
optionC: A connection to the internet
optionD: Both machines to be made by the same manufacturer
correctAnswerText: A connection between them and an agreed way of addressing each other
explanation: A network is machines connected with a shared way of finding one another. The internet is one very large example rather than a requirement, and a browser is one program among many that uses a network.

prompt: Two machines in one room are connected to each other and to nothing else. Is that a network?
optionA: No; a network must reach the internet
optionB: No; two machines are too few
optionC: Yes, but only while data is actually moving
optionD: Yes; connected machines that can exchange data form a network whatever its size
correctAnswerText: Yes; connected machines that can exchange data form a network whatever its size
explanation: What makes a network is the connection and the ability to exchange, not the scale or the reach. A network with no traffic is idle rather than nonexistent.

prompt: Must both machines be switched on at the same moment for any exchange to be possible?
optionA: For a direct exchange yes; a message left with an intermediary can be collected later
optionB: Yes, always; data cannot be held anywhere
optionC: No; data waits on the network until the other machine appears
optionD: No; the network stores everything sent over it
correctAnswerText: For a direct exchange yes; a message left with an intermediary can be collected later
explanation: A direct conversation needs both ends present, and services that hold messages exist precisely so that they do not have to be. The network itself carries rather than stores.

prompt: Is the internet the same thing as a network?
optionA: Yes; the two words mean the same thing
optionB: No; a network is part of a computer and the internet is outside it
optionC: No; the internet is a very large network built out of many smaller ones
optionD: Yes; every network is connected to the internet
correctAnswerText: No; the internet is a very large network built out of many smaller ones
explanation: Networks exist at every scale and most are not connected to the internet at all. Treating the two as synonyms makes a disconnected office network impossible to describe.

prompt: A machine is connected to a network and cannot reach any other machine on it. What has to be true for it to succeed?
optionA: It must have a browser installed
optionB: It must be able to address the other machine and have a path to it
optionC: It must be the same kind of machine as the others
optionD: It must be switched on before the others
correctAnswerText: It must be able to address the other machine and have a path to it
explanation: Reaching another machine needs both a way to name it and a route that carries the data. A physical connection alone is not enough if either is missing.

prompt: Which does a network use to decide where to send data?
optionA: The name
optionB: Either; they are interchangeable
optionC: The name, converted to uppercase
optionD: The address
correctAnswerText: The address
explanation: Routing works on addresses, and a name has to be looked up to obtain one first. The two exist for different audiences: names for people, addresses for machines.

prompt: What is a name used for?
optionA: So that people can refer to a machine without remembering its address
optionB: So that the network can route data
optionC: So that the machine can identify itself to its operating system
optionD: So that two machines can share one address
correctAnswerText: So that people can refer to a machine without remembering its address
explanation: A name is a convenience for people, resolved to an address before anything is sent. The network never sees it.

prompt: Does one name always refer to the same machine?
optionA: Yes; a name is permanently tied to one machine
optionB: Yes, unless the machine is switched off
optionC: No; the address a name points at can be changed at any time
optionD: No; a name refers to a different machine on each request
correctAnswerText: No; the address a name points at can be changed at any time
explanation: The point of a name is that it can be redirected, which is how a service moves to new hardware without anybody learning a new address. It does not change on its own between requests.

prompt: A name is entered in a browser. What has to happen before any data is sent to that machine?
optionA: The data is sent to the name and forwarded
optionB: The name is looked up to obtain an address
optionC: The machine announces its address to the browser
optionD: Nothing; names are routable in the same way as addresses
correctAnswerText: The name is looked up to obtain an address
explanation: Nothing can be routed until an address exists, so the lookup happens first. Sending to a name would require every machine on the path to understand names.

prompt: What does a port identify?
optionA: Which machine the data is for
optionB: A physical socket the cable plugs into
optionC: How fast the data may be sent
optionD: Which service on a machine the data is for
correctAnswerText: Which service on a machine the data is for
explanation: The address gets data to the machine and the port decides which program on it receives them. The physical socket is a different thing that happens to share the word.

prompt: Two services on one machine try to use the same port. What happens?
optionA: One of them fails to start, because a port can serve only one at a time
optionB: Both work, sharing the port
optionC: Both fail to start
optionD: The machine chooses a different port for one of them automatically
correctAnswerText: One of them fails to start, because a port can serve only one at a time
explanation: A port has to identify one recipient unambiguously, so a second claim on it is refused. Nothing reassigns it, which is why the second service reports that the port is in use.

prompt: Can two different machines each run a service on the same port number?
optionA: No; a port number may be used once anywhere
optionB: Yes, but only if the machines are on different networks
optionC: Yes; the port only has to be unique on its own machine
optionD: No; port numbers are assigned centrally
correctAnswerText: Yes; the port only has to be unique on its own machine
explanation: A recipient is identified by an address and a port together, so the same port on two machines is two different destinations. That is why every web server can use the same port.

prompt: A developer starts a second copy of their application and it reports that the port is already in use. What is happening?
optionA: The machine has run out of ports
optionB: The first copy still holds the port, and only one service may hold it at a time
optionC: The application cannot be run twice on any machine
optionD: The port number is reserved by the operating system
correctAnswerText: The first copy still holds the port, and only one service may hold it at a time
explanation: The first copy is still running and still holding its port. Starting a second on a different port works perfectly well, which shows the limit is the port rather than the application.

prompt: Put the steps of reaching a named machine in order.
optionA: Connect to the name, look up the address, exchange data
optionB: Exchange data with the name, which forwards it
optionC: Look the name up once for all sites, then connect
optionD: Look the name up, obtain an address, connect to that address, exchange data
correctAnswerText: Look the name up, obtain an address, connect to that address, exchange data
explanation: A connection needs an address, so the lookup comes first. Looking up once for everything would require knowing every site to be visited in advance.

prompt: A machine visits two different named sites. How many lookups are needed?
optionA: One per name, though a remembered result may be reused
optionB: One in total, covering both
optionC: One per request, always
optionD: None; the addresses are already known
correctAnswerText: One per name, though a remembered result may be reused
explanation: Each name needs its own address, and results are commonly remembered for a while so a repeat visit may need no lookup. Neither extreme — one lookup for everything, or one for every request — describes what happens.

prompt: A developer runs a service and reaches it at an address meaning "this machine". Can a colleague use that same address to reach it?
optionA: Yes; the address identifies the developer's machine
optionB: Yes, if they are on the same network
optionC: No; on the colleague's machine that address means their own machine
optionD: No; the colleague needs the same browser
correctAnswerText: No; on the colleague's machine that address means their own machine
explanation: An address meaning "this machine" is relative to whoever uses it, so it never points anywhere else. Sharing it sends the colleague to their own machine, where nothing is listening.

prompt: A service is reachable from other machines in the same office and not from outside. What does that tell you about its address?
optionA: It is a public address that has been blocked
optionB: It is an address meaningful only within that network, not reachable from the wider internet
optionC: It is an address meaning "this machine"
optionD: It has no address, only a name
correctAnswerText: It is an address meaningful only within that network, not reachable from the wider internet
explanation: Working across the office rules out an address meaning "this machine", and failing outside points at a range that is valid only within a network. Many networks reuse the same such ranges, which is why they cannot be routed globally.

prompt: A large file is sent across a network. How does it travel?
optionA: As one continuous unit from start to finish
optionB: As one piece per second, regardless of size
optionC: Compressed into a single small piece
optionD: Divided into many small pieces sent separately
correctAnswerText: Divided into many small pieces sent separately
explanation: Data is broken into pieces so that a network can interleave traffic from many sources. Sending a large file as one unit would block everything else for its duration.

prompt: The pieces of one file arrive at the destination out of order. What must happen?
optionA: The receiver reassembles them into the right order using information each piece carries
optionB: The whole file must be sent again
optionC: The pieces are used in the order they arrive
optionD: Out-of-order arrival is impossible
correctAnswerText: The receiver reassembles them into the right order using information each piece carries
explanation: Pieces may take different routes and arrive in any order, so each carries enough to place it. Reassembly is the receiver's job and is why arriving out of order is ordinary rather than a failure.

prompt: One piece of a file is lost in transit and the file arrives complete anyway. Nothing was sent again by the application. What happened?
optionA: The receiver reconstructed the missing piece from the others
optionB: The piece was not really lost
optionC: The layer below the application noticed the loss and sent that piece again
optionD: The file was small enough not to need that piece
correctAnswerText: The layer below the application noticed the loss and sent that piece again
explanation: The application seeing a complete file while a piece was lost means something below it handled the loss. Reconstructing missing data from the rest is not something an ordinary transfer does.

prompt: A file is being downloaded. Which kind of delivery suits it?
optionA: One that sends pieces once and accepts losses
optionB: One that guarantees every piece arrives, resending anything lost
optionC: One that sends every piece twice
optionD: Either; a file is unaffected by losses
correctAnswerText: One that guarantees every piece arrives, resending anything lost
explanation: A file with a missing piece is corrupt, so completeness matters more than timing. Accepting losses would produce a file that is quietly wrong.

prompt: A live video call is in progress. Which kind of delivery suits it, and what is given up?
optionA: One that guarantees delivery, giving up nothing
optionB: One that guarantees delivery, giving up bandwidth
optionC: Either; the choice affects only cost
optionD: One that accepts losses, giving up perfect quality to avoid waiting for resends
correctAnswerText: One that accepts losses, giving up perfect quality to avoid waiting for resends
explanation: A piece resent arrives too late to be shown, so waiting for it delays everything after it. A brief glitch is preferable to a call that falls steadily further behind.

prompt: A team uses guaranteed delivery for a live audio stream and users report that the audio drifts further and further behind. The connection loses a small number of pieces. Why does the guarantee hurt here?
optionA: Every lost piece is resent and everything after it waits, so the delay accumulates
optionB: The guarantee makes each piece larger
optionC: The guarantee sends every piece twice
optionD: The guarantee is unrelated; the network is simply slow
correctAnswerText: Every lost piece is resent and everything after it waits, so the delay accumulates
explanation: Guaranteed delivery preserves order as well as completeness, so a resend holds up what follows it. Losses that would have been an inaudible glitch become a growing lag instead.

prompt: Data sent from one machine to another across the internet travels how?
optionA: Directly, over a dedicated connection between the two
optionB: Through one intermediate machine, always
optionC: Through a series of intermediate machines that pass it along
optionD: Through every machine on the internet
correctAnswerText: Through a series of intermediate machines that pass it along
explanation: A path is built from many hops, each forwarding towards the destination. A dedicated connection between every pair of machines would need an impossible number of links.

prompt: What do the intermediate machines along a path do with the data?
optionA: Read the content to decide where to send it
optionB: Forward it towards its destination, without needing to understand its content
optionC: Store a copy of everything they forward
optionD: Rewrite the content for the next machine
correctAnswerText: Forward it towards its destination, without needing to understand its content
explanation: Forwarding needs the destination address and nothing more, which is what makes the same machines able to carry any kind of traffic. Reading the content would be a separate act rather than a requirement of forwarding.

prompt: A measurement shows data taking one route from A to B and a different route from B back to A. Both directions work correctly. Is that a fault?
optionA: Yes; a connection must use one path in both directions
optionB: Yes; different paths mean one of them is misconfigured
optionC: No; but only because the measurement is unreliable
optionD: No; each direction is routed independently and the paths need not match
correctAnswerText: No; each direction is routed independently and the paths need not match
explanation: Routing decisions are made hop by hop for each direction, so asymmetry is ordinary. Expecting a single shared path treats a route as a physical circuit rather than a series of independent decisions.

prompt: Which responsibility covers getting data to the right machine?
optionA: Addressing and routing
optionB: Resending anything lost
optionC: Deciding what the data means
optionD: Encrypting the data
correctAnswerText: Addressing and routing
explanation: Each responsibility is a separate job and this one is about destination. Resending is about reliability and meaning belongs to whatever produced the data.

prompt: Which responsibility covers noticing that a piece did not arrive and sending it again?
optionA: Addressing and routing
optionB: Deciding what the data means
optionC: Reliable delivery
optionD: Choosing which service receives it
correctAnswerText: Reliable delivery
explanation: Detecting loss and repairing it is a distinct job from getting data to a machine. Routing delivers what it can and reports nothing about what went missing.

prompt: A team argues that encryption belongs to routing, because routing is what moves the data. Encryption can be applied without changing how anything is routed. Where does it belong?
optionA: To routing, since routing moves the data
optionB: To a separate responsibility, since routed data is carried unchanged whether or not it is encrypted
optionC: To reliable delivery, since encryption protects data
optionD: To addressing, since encrypted data still needs an address
correctAnswerText: To a separate responsibility, since routed data is carried unchanged whether or not it is encrypted
explanation: Responsibilities are separated by what would have to change if one were altered, and encrypting changes nothing about how data is addressed or forwarded. That independence is what makes it a separate concern.

prompt: A large file downloads slowly but steadily. Which is the limit?
optionA: Delay — how long each piece takes to arrive
optionB: Neither; the file is simply large
optionC: Both equally
optionD: Capacity — how much can travel per second
correctAnswerText: Capacity — how much can travel per second
explanation: A steady transfer that takes a long time is limited by how much can flow at once. Delay affects how soon the first piece appears rather than how fast the bulk arrives.

prompt: A remote application feels sluggish: every click takes a noticeable moment to respond, though large files download quickly. Which is the limit?
optionA: Delay — each exchange takes time regardless of how little data it carries
optionB: Capacity, which must be low
optionC: Neither; the application is slow
optionD: Both, since they are the same quantity
correctAnswerText: Delay — each exchange takes time regardless of how little data it carries
explanation: Fast downloads show capacity is ample, and a pause on every small exchange is what delay produces. The two are separate quantities and are commonly collapsed into the single word "speed".

prompt: A team buys a much larger connection to fix an application that felt sluggish, and it feels exactly the same. Downloads were already fast before the upgrade. What was the real limit?
optionA: Capacity, and the new connection is faulty
optionB: The application, which cannot use the extra capacity
optionC: Delay, which a larger connection does not reduce
optionD: The number of users sharing the connection
correctAnswerText: Delay, which a larger connection does not reduce
explanation: Downloads already being fast showed capacity was not the constraint, so buying more of it changed nothing. Delay is a property of distance and the path rather than of how much can flow at once.

prompt: A name is pointed at a new address. When does everyone start reaching the new machine?
optionA: Immediately everywhere
optionB: Gradually, as remembered results expire in different places
optionC: Never; the old address is permanent
optionD: When every affected machine is restarted
correctAnswerText: Gradually, as remembered results expire in different places
explanation: Lookup results are remembered for a period that differs by location, so the change spreads rather than switching. That is why a move is planned around the remembering period.

prompt: After a name is repointed, some users reach the new machine and others the old one. Both machines are running and both answer correctly. Where is the difference?
optionA: In the browsers, which are caching the page
optionB: In the servers, one of which is misconfigured
optionC: In the users' network connections
optionD: In how recently each user's lookup result was obtained
correctAnswerText: In how recently each user's lookup result was obtained
explanation: Both machines answering rules out a misconfiguration, and the split is by which address each user resolved. A browser cache would produce a stale page rather than a connection to a different machine.

prompt: A service is unreachable from an office network and reachable from a home connection. The service is the same in both cases. Where is the block?
optionA: On the office network, which is preventing the connection
optionB: On the server, which is refusing the office
optionC: In the name lookup, which fails at the office
optionD: In the application, which behaves differently at the office
correctAnswerText: On the office network, which is preventing the connection
explanation: The service answering from elsewhere shows it is running and reachable, so what differs is the network in between. A server refusing one network specifically is possible and far less likely than a network restricting outbound access.

prompt: A connection to a service fails from one network. The name resolves correctly there, and the same address is reachable from another network. Which stage is failing?
optionA: The name lookup, which must be returning the wrong address
optionB: The server, which must be down
optionC: The connection itself, after the address is known — something on the path is refusing it
optionD: The application, which must be rejecting the request
correctAnswerText: The connection itself, after the address is known — something on the path is refusing it
explanation: A correct lookup rules out the naming stage, and reachability from elsewhere rules out the server. What is left is the path between this network and the service.

prompt: A connection attempt reports that the name could not be found. Which stage failed?
optionA: The connection, which was refused
optionB: The lookup, before any connection was attempted
optionC: The server, which did not answer
optionD: The application, which rejected the request
correctAnswerText: The lookup, before any connection was attempted
explanation: Failing to find a name means no address was obtained, so nothing was ever sent. Every later stage requires an address to exist.

prompt: A connection attempt reports that it was refused. The name resolved to an address without any trouble. Which stage failed?
optionA: The lookup, which returned nothing
optionB: The application, which returned an error
optionC: Nothing; a refusal is a normal response
optionD: The connection, because something at the address actively declined it
correctAnswerText: The connection, because something at the address actively declined it
explanation: A refusal means the address was reached and something answered by declining, which places the failure after the lookup and before any application exchange. An application error would have required a connection to succeed first.

prompt: A connection attempt resolves the name and then simply waits, with no refusal and no answer. What are the two likely causes, and what would separate them?
optionA: Nothing is listening at that address, or something silently discards the traffic; whether the address is reachable at all separates them
optionB: The name is wrong, or the server is down; a second lookup separates them
optionC: The application is slow, or the file is large; waiting longer separates them
optionD: There is only one cause: the server is down
correctAnswerText: Nothing is listening at that address, or something silently discards the traffic; whether the address is reachable at all separates them
explanation: A refusal means something answered, and silence means nothing did — which happens both when the address is unreachable and when traffic is dropped on the way. Establishing whether the address responds to anything at all is what tells them apart.

prompt: A connection succeeds and the reply takes eight seconds. Is that a connection failure?
optionA: Yes; a slow reply is a failed connection
optionB: Yes; the connection must have been retried several times
optionC: No; the connection worked and something after it is slow, which is a different investigation
optionD: No; eight seconds is normal for any network
correctAnswerText: No; the connection worked and something after it is slow, which is a different investigation
explanation: A slow answer is an answer, so every stage of connecting succeeded. Treating slowness as failure sends the investigation to the network when the delay may be entirely in the application.

prompt: Three failures produce three different symptoms: a name that cannot be found, a refusal, and silence. Why is that useful?
optionA: It is not useful; all three mean the service is unavailable
optionB: Each symptom names a different stage, so the symptom alone narrows the investigation before anything is tried
optionC: It is useful only because the messages can be searched for
optionD: It is useful because each has a standard fix
correctAnswerText: Each symptom names a different stage, so the symptom alone narrows the investigation before anything is tried
explanation: The stages fail in observably different ways, which turns the first symptom into evidence about where to look. Treating all three as "unavailable" discards that information at the outset.

prompt: A password is sent over an unencrypted connection on a shared network. The page looked ordinary and nothing appeared to go wrong. What can someone on the same network learn?
optionA: Only which site was contacted
optionB: Nothing, since the data is in pieces
optionC: Only the length of what was sent
optionD: The password itself, along with everything else that was sent
correctAnswerText: The password itself, along with everything else that was sent
explanation: Without encryption the contents travel in the clear and anyone on the path can read them. That the exchange looked ordinary is exactly why the risk is invisible to the user.

prompt: The connection is encrypted. What can someone on the path still learn?
optionA: Which host was contacted, roughly how much was exchanged and when
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: The full contents, but not who sent them
optionD: Only whether the connection succeeded
correctAnswerText: Which host was contacted, roughly how much was exchanged and when
explanation: Encryption conceals the contents and leaves the shape of the traffic visible — who was contacted, how much and when. Claiming nothing is visible is the overstatement that leads people to rely on it too far.

prompt: A user believes a private home network makes their traffic unreadable. Is that so?
optionA: Yes; a private network is not visible to others
optionB: Yes, provided nobody else knows the network password
optionC: No; the traffic leaves the network and is readable on the path unless it is encrypted
optionD: No; but only for traffic to sites in other countries
correctAnswerText: No; the traffic leaves the network and is readable on the path unless it is encrypted
explanation: A private network controls who can join it and nothing about what happens once traffic leaves. The protection people are relying on is encryption, which is a separate matter from the network being private.

prompt: A page shows a padlock and a user concludes the site is safe to give their bank details to. What has the padlock actually established?
optionA: That the site is trustworthy
optionB: That the connection is encrypted and the site is the one the name refers to — not that the operator is honest
optionC: That the site is a bank
optionD: That the data will be stored securely
correctAnswerText: That the connection is encrypted and the site is the one the name refers to — not that the operator is honest
explanation: The indicator says the exchange is protected and the name matches, which any site including a fraudulent one can obtain. Nothing about it speaks to what happens to the data afterwards.

prompt: Encrypting traffic costs a little time on every exchange. When is that cost not worth paying?
optionA: Whenever the data is not secret
optionB: Whenever the network is private
optionC: Whenever the connection is already slow
optionD: Almost never for anything crossing a network; the cost is small and the alternative is exposure of everything sent
correctAnswerText: Almost never for anything crossing a network; the cost is small and the alternative is exposure of everything sent
explanation: The cost is a small and fixed overhead, and the exposure it prevents applies to everything including data nobody thought was sensitive. Judging each exchange separately is how credentials end up travelling in the clear.

prompt: A service runs on a developer's machine and must be reachable by a colleague in the same office. Sharing the local address did not work. What must change?
optionA: The colleague must use the machine's address on the office network, and the service must accept connections from it
optionB: The colleague must use the same local address
optionC: The service must be moved to a different port
optionD: The colleague must install the same browser
correctAnswerText: The colleague must use the machine's address on the office network, and the service must accept connections from it
explanation: A local address means "this machine" wherever it is used, so it can never point at somebody else's. What is needed is an address that identifies the machine on the shared network, and a service willing to answer on it.

prompt: The same service must now be reachable from the internet. What is needed beyond an office address?
optionA: A public name pointing at the office address
optionB: A different port number
optionC: An address reachable from outside, and a path opened to it through whatever stands in the way
optionD: Nothing further; office addresses are reachable from anywhere
correctAnswerText: An address reachable from outside, and a path opened to it through whatever stands in the way
explanation: An address valid only within a network cannot be routed from outside, so a reachable address comes first and a path through has to be opened. A name pointing at an unreachable address resolves and still fails.

prompt: A public name is created and points at the service's address, and it is still unreachable from outside. What does that show about names?
optionA: The name was created incorrectly
optionB: A name only supplies an address; it cannot make an unreachable address reachable
optionC: Names take time to work and this one is not ready
optionD: The service must be restarted for the name to take effect
correctAnswerText: A name only supplies an address; it cannot make an unreachable address reachable
explanation: Resolution and reachability are separate stages, and a name settles only the first. Propagation delay is real and would produce the same symptom, which is why the address itself has to be checked rather than assumed.

prompt: Making a local service reachable from the internet is easy to do and easy to do badly. What is the trade?
optionA: There is no trade; reachability is simply a setting
optionB: It costs only performance, since more traffic arrives
optionC: It costs only the effort of configuring it
optionD: It gains access for anyone who needs it and exposes the service to everyone else, so what it accepts has to be considered
correctAnswerText: It gains access for anyone who needs it and exposes the service to everyone else, so what it accepts has to be considered
explanation: Opening a path does not distinguish between the colleague who needs access and everything else that will find it. The cost is not effort or speed but that the service now answers to the whole internet.
